title: Rewarding Disagreement
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Argues that good leaders invite disagreement but great leaders reward it, by telling people explicitly how their counterarguments changed the leader's opinion or decision. The post frames disagreement as the raw material of quality decisions and false consensus as the risk of a leader who never hears dissent. The move is from tolerating dissent (tempering reactions, asking people to elaborate) to visibly crediting it. Showing team members that candor has an impact on process and outcome teaches them that honesty pays, so they keep offering it. The closing line sets agreement as the foundation of consensus and disagreement as the cornerstone of good decisions.
points: Inviting dissent is not enough; the highest reward a leader can give is to report back how a contrary view changed their thinking.
Without people willing to disagree, leaders operate in a vacuum of false consensus that deprives them of counterarguments.
Tempering your reaction and asking people to expound before debating signals that all views will be considered.
Rewarded disagreement becomes self-reinforcing: once people see their candor matters, they rarely stop offering it.
quotes: Good leaders encourage those around them to disagree, candidly offering an opposing view whenever they have one. They explicitly tell colleagues they want their disagreement, and they do their best to embolden them by tempering their reactions to any opposing viewpoints.

When team members are shown that their contributions have positively influenced the leader, they begin to see honest disagreement in a different light. Learning that they can have an impact on both the process and outcome, team members who openly disagree experience the value they provide by being candid.

Great leaders light a perpetual fire when they go out of their way to describe this kind of influence. Not surprisingly, such a reward promotes more disagreement and candidness. To the delight of an exceptional leader, once team members are rewarded for disagreeing, they rarely stop.

While asking for and even seeking disagreement encourages team members to step up and offer a contrary view when they have one, the real reward occurs when leaders incorporate the counterarguments into their thinking. Telling team members that what they have said and the points they offered have made an impact on how the leader now views the issue is the highest prize.
Just as agreement is the foundation of consensus, disagreement is the cornerstone of quality decision-making. Without it, leaders are defenseless against their own opinions.
